The **Yakuts** or **Sakha** ([Yakut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakut_language "Yakut language"): саха _saxa_ ; plural: сахалар _saxalar_) are a [Turkic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkic_peoples "Turkic peoples") ethnic group native to North Siberia, primarily the [Republic of Sakha (Yakutia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sakha_Republic "Sakha Republic") in the [Russian Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia"). They also inhabit some districts of the [Krasnoyarsk Krai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krasnoyarsk_Krai "Krasnoyarsk Krai"). They speak [Yakut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakut_language "Yakut language"), which belongs to the [Siberian branch of the Turkic languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siberian_Turkic_languages "Siberian Turkic languages").
## Etymology
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakuts&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]
According to Yakut philosopher Alexey Kulakovsky,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-4) the Russian word _yakut_ was taken from the [Evenki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evenki_language "Evenki language") екэ, _yekə̄_[Tungusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tungusic_languages "Tungusic languages") form.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-5) According to ethnographer [Dávid Somfai Kara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%A1vid_Somfai_Kara "Dávid Somfai Kara"), the Russian _yakut_ derives from the [Buryat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buryat_language "Buryat language") _yaqud_ , which is the plural form of the Buryat name for the Yakuts, _yaqa_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-6) The Yakuts call themselves _Sakha_.
## Origin
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakuts&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Origin")]
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/%D0%9A%D0%BE%D0%BB%D0%BB%D0%B0%D0%B6_%D0%B8%D0%B7_%D1%84%D0%BE%D1%82%D0%BE%D0%B3%D1%80%D0%B0%D1%84%D0%B8%D0%B9_%D0%B8%D0%B7%D0%B2%D0%B5%D1%81%D1%82%D0%BD%D1%8B%D1%85_%D0%BB%D1%8E%D0%B4%D0%B5%D0%B9_%D1%8F%D0%BA%D1%83%D1%82%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%B3%D0%BE_%D0%BF%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%B8%D1%81%D1%85%D0%BE%D0%B6%D0%B4%D0%B5%D0%BD%D0%B8%D1%8F.png/250px-%D0%9A%D0%BE%D0%BB%D0%BB%D0%B0%D0%B6_%D0%B8%D0%B7_%D1%84%D0%BE%D1%82%D0%BE%D0%B3%D1%80%D0%B0%D1%84%D0%B8%D0%B9_%D0%B8%D0%B7%D0%B2%D0%B5%D1%81%D1%82%D0%BD%D1%8B%D1%85_%D0%BB%D1%8E%D0%B4%D0%B5%D0%B9_%D1%8F%D0%BA%D1%83%D1%82%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%B3%D0%BE_%D0%BF%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%B8%D1%81%D1%85%D0%BE%D0%B6%D0%B4%D0%B5%D0%BD%D0%B8%D1%8F.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:%D0%9A%D0%BE%D0%BB%D0%BB%D0%B0%D0%B6_%D0%B8%D0%B7_%D1%84%D0%BE%D1%82%D0%BE%D0%B3%D1%80%D0%B0%D1%84%D0%B8%D0%B9_%D0%B8%D0%B7%D0%B2%D0%B5%D1%81%D1%82%D0%BD%D1%8B%D1%85_%D0%BB%D1%8E%D0%B4%D0%B5%D0%B9_%D1%8F%D0%BA%D1%83%D1%82%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%B3%D0%BE_%D0%BF%D1%80%D0%BE%D0%B8%D1%81%D1%85%D0%BE%D0%B6%D0%B4%D0%B5%D0%BD%D0%B8%D1%8F.png)Famous Yakuts
An early work on Yakut ethnogenesis was drafted by the Russian [Collegiate Assessors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collegiate_Assessor "Collegiate Assessor") I. Evers and S. Gornovsky in the late 18th century. At an unspecified time in the past certain tribes resided around the western shore of the [Aral Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aral_Sea "Aral Sea"). These peoples later migrated eastward and settled near the [Tunka Goltsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tunka_Goltsy "Tunka Goltsy") mountains of modern [Buryatia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buryatia "Buryatia"). Pressure from the expansionist Mongolian Empire later made many of those around the Tunka Goltsy relocate to the Lena River. Several additional [Altai-Sayan region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altai-Sayan_region "Altai-Sayan region") tribes later arrived on the Lena to flee from the Mongols. The subsequent cultural melding that occurred between these incoming migrants eventually created the Yakuts. The Sagay [Khakas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khakas "Khakas") of [Abakan River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abakan_\(river\) "Abakan \(river\)") were presented as the origin of the ethnonym Sakha by Evers and Gornovsky.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEIvanov1974168%E2%80%93170-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUshnitskiy2016a150-8)
In the mid-19th century, Nikolai S. Schukin wrote "A Trip to Yakutsk" based on his experiences visiting the area. He presented a somewhat different origin of the Yakuts that is based upon local oral histories. Groups of Khakas inhabiting the southern [Yenisey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yenisey "Yenisey") watershed migrated north to the [Nizhnyaya Tunguska River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nizhnyaya_Tunguska_River "Nizhnyaya Tunguska River") to the [Lena Plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lena_Plateau "Lena Plateau") and finally onward to the Lena River.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTESchukin1844273%E2%80%93274-9) Schukin is credited as introducing the concept of Yenisey Khakas as the ancestors of the Yakut into Russian historiography.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKsenofontov199272-10) The most authoritative account in support of the Yenisey origin hypothesis was written by Nikolai N. Kozmin in 1928.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKsenofontov1992108-11) He concluded that some Khakas moved from the Yenisey to the [Angara River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angara_River "Angara River") due to difficulties in the regional economy. In the 12th century, Buryats arrived at [Lake Baikal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Baikal "Lake Baikal") and through military force pushed the Khakas to the Lena.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKozmin1928273-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEUshnitskiy2016a152-13)
### Lake Baikal
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakuts&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Lake Baikal")]
In 1893, Turkologist scholar [Vasily Radlov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasily_Radlov "Vasily Radlov") connected the [Kurykans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurykans "Kurykans") or _Gǔlìgān_ ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language"): ) [Tiele people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiele_people "Tiele people") from Chinese historical accounts with the Yakuts. They are mentioned as 7th-century tributaries of the [Tang dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tang_dynasty "Tang dynasty"), reportedly living on the Angara and around Lake Baikal. Radlov hypothesized they were a mixture of Tungusic and Uyghur peoples and the forebears of the Yakut.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTERadlov1893134-14)
### Khoro
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakuts&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Khoro")]
The Khoro (Khorin, Khorolors, Khori) Sakha maintain their progenitor was Uluu Khoro, rather than Omogoy or Ellei. Scholarship has not definitively established their ancestral ethnic affiliations. Their homeland was somewhere in the south and called Khoro sire. When the Khorolors arrived in the Middle Lena remains uncertain, with scholars estimating from the first millennium to the 16th century AD.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZoriktuev2011-15)
Among scholars a commonly accepted hypothesis is that the Khoro Yakut originate from the Khori Buryat of Lake Baikal,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTERumyantsev1962144-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOvchinnikov1897-17) and therefore spoke a Turko-Mongolic language.[_[according to whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Words_to_watch#Unsupported_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_][[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTENimaev1988108-18) This is largely based on their similar ethnonyms. Proponents see the word Khoro as arising from the Tibetan word hor ([Standard Tibetan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Tibetan_language "Standard Tibetan language"): [ཧོར](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E0%BD%A7%E0%BD%BC%E0%BD%A2 "wikt:ཧོར")[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKarmay1993244-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_Roerich199942-20) For example, according to G. N. Rumyanstev, during the 6th through 10th centuries CE the inhabitants of Lake Baikal were called Chor.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTERumyantsev1962127%E2%80%93128-21) Okladnikov guessed that Khoro sire was near China and adjacent to the X.[_[vague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Vagueness "Wikipedia:Vagueness")_]
This premise is not universally accepted and has been challenged by some researchers.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDashieva2020943%E2%80%93944-22) [George de Roerich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_de_Roerich "George de Roerich") has argued that the word is based on the Chinese word hu ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language"): [胡](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%E8%83%A1 "wikt:胡")), a term used as general reference by the Chinese to refer to nomadic Mongolic peoples of Central Asia. In contemporary Tibetan hor is used to describe any pastoralist "nomad of mixed origin" regardless of their ethnonym.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEde_Roerich199989-23) After researching their origins, [Gavriil Ksenofontov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavriil_Ksenofontov "Gavriil Ksenofontov") concluded that while the Khorolors were "formed from parts of some alien tribe that mixed with the Yakuts", there was no compelling evidence connecting them with the Khori Buryat.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZoriktuev2011120-24)
A more recent argument by Zoriktuev proposes that the Khorolors were originally Paleo-Asians from the Lower Amur River.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEZoriktuev2011-15) In contrast to their Yakut relatives, Khoro folklore focuses largely on the Raven, with some tales about the Eagle as well. In the mid 18th century Lindenau noted the Khorolors focused their religious devotion on the Raven,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTELindenau198318-25) who was alternatively referred to as "Our ancestor", "Our deity", and "Our grandfather" by the Khorolors. This reverence arises from the Raven enabling a struggling human (either the first Khoro man or his mother) to survive by giving a flint and tinder box. Their mythos is similar to cultures from both sides of the Bering Sea.[_[according to whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Words_to_watch#Unsupported_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] The Haida, Tlingit, Tshisham of the North American Pacific Northwest Coast and the Paleoasians of the Siberian Coast like the Chukchi, Itelmen, and Koryaks all share reverence for the Raven.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKrasheninnikov1949406-26)
### Autochthonous ancestry
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakuts&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Autochthonous ancestry")]
Many researchers have concluded that the Yakut ethnogenesis was an admixture of Turks migrating from Lake-Baikal and native Yukaghir and Tungusitic peoples residing around the Lena River.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTETokarev1949-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOkladnikov1955-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKonstantinov1978-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGogolev1993-30) Okladnikov detailed this conceived admixture process as the following:
> "...the Turkic-speaking ancestors of the Yakuts not only pushed out the aborigines but also subjected them to their influence by peaceful means; they assimilated and absorbed them into their mass... With this, the local tribes lost the former ethnic name and a proper ethnic consciousness, no longer separating themselves from the mass of Yakuts, and [were] not opposed to them... Consequently, as a result of the mixing with Northern aborigines, the southern ancestors of the Yakuts supplemented their culture and language with new features distinguishing them from other steppe tribes."
Traditional Yakut histories contain stories of the aboriginal peoples of Yakutia. From the [subarctic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subarctic "Subarctic") [Bulunsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulunsky_District "Bulunsky District") and [Verkhoyansky Districts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verkhoyansky_District "Verkhoyansky District"), accounts state that the Black Yukaghir (Yakut: хара дъукаагырдар) descended from migrants pushed north from the Lena River.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEErgis1960282-31) Related stories recorded in [Ust'-Aldanskiy Ulus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ust'-Aldanskiy_Ulus "Ust'-Aldanskiy Ulus") and [Megino-Kangalassky District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megino-Kangalassky_District "Megino-Kangalassky District") mention certain tribes leaving the region due to rising pressure from the incoming Yakuts. While some remained and intermarried with the newcomer, most went to the northern tundra.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEErgis196092%E2%80%9393-32)
#### Ymyyakhtakh
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakuts&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Ymyyakhtakh")]
The [Ymyyakhtakh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ymyyakhtakh_culture "Ymyyakhtakh culture") are an ancient people of the Lena River.[_[according to whom?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Words_to_watch#Unsupported_attributions "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Words to watch")_] A burial ground was excavated[_[when?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_] and anthropologists I.I. Gokhman and L.F. Tomtosova studied the human remains and published their results in 1992. They concluded that some of the Late Neolithic population took part in the formation of the modern Yakuts.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGokhmanTomtosova1992117-33) The consistency of related artistic embellishments on the traditional clothing of the Buryat, Samoyed, and Yakut led one scholar to conclude they are related.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPavlinskaya2001231-34) Toponymic data of Yakutia indicates there was once a presence of Paleoasian and Samoyed habitation in the region.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEStepanov2005-35) Vilyui Tumats reportedly practiced [anthropophagy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_cannibalism "Human cannibalism") and seen as an "ethnocultural marker" of the Samoyedic peoples.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBravinaPetrov2018121%E2%80%93122-36)
#### Tumats
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakuts&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Tumats")]
The Tumat stand out in Yakut tradition as a numerous and powerful society, with constant conflict once happening with them on the [Vilyuy River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vilyuy_River "Vilyuy River").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEErgis1960103-37) Their households were semi-subterranean with sod roofing and are comparable to traditional Samoyed dwellings.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBravinaPetrov2018120-38) The term Doubo ([Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language"): ) was used in medieval Chinese historical works in reference to the Sayano-Altai forest peoples. [Vasily Radlov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasily_Radlov "Vasily Radlov") concluded that Doubo referred to the Samoyedic peoples.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTERadlov1893191-39) Doubo is additionally seen as the origin of the ethnonym "Tumat" by L. P. Potapov.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPotapov1969182-40)
The Yakuts called the Tumat people "Dyirikinei" or "chipmunk people" (Yakut: Sдьирикинэй), arising from the Tumatian "tail-coat." Bundles of deer fur were dyed with red ocher and sewn into Tumatian jackets as adornments. Tumat hats were likewise dyed red.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOkladnikov1955339-41) This style was likely spread by the Tumatians to some Tungusic peoples. Similar clothing has been reported during the 17th century for the Evenks on the upper Angara and for Evens residing on the lower Kolyma in the early 19th century.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTETugolukov1985216,_235-42) Additionally there are many similarities between the clothing of the Tumats and Altaic cultures. Archeological work on [Pazyryk culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pazyryk_culture "Pazyryk culture") sites have turned up both hats dyed red and tail-coats made of sables. While the "tails" were not dyed red, they were sewn with red dyed thread. Stylistic and design choices are also comparable to traditional [Khakas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khakas "Khakas") and [Kumandin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kumandin "Kumandin") clothing.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBravinaPetrov2018121-43)
Some peaceable interactions including intermarriage did occur with the Tumats. One such example is the life of Džaardaakh ([Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_language "Russian language"): Джаардаах[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKsenofontov1977206-44) The origin of her name has been linked to a Yukaghir word for ice (Yukaghir: йархан).[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEIvanov200019-45)
The ancestors of Yakuts were [Kurykans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurykans "Kurykans") who migrated from [Yenisey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yenisey "Yenisey") river to [Lake Baikal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Baikal "Lake Baikal") and were subject to a certain Mongolian admixture prior to migration in the 7th century.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKhar'kovStepanovMedvedevSpiridonova2008-46) The Yakuts originally lived around [Olkhon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olkhon "Olkhon") and the region of [Lake Baikal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Baikal "Lake Baikal"). Beginning in the 13th century they migrated to the basins of the Middle [Lena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lena_River "Lena River"), the [Aldan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aldan_River "Aldan River") and [Vilyuy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vilyuy_River "Vilyuy River") rivers under the pressure of the rising [Mongols](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol "Mongol"). The northern Yakuts were largely hunters, fishermen and [reindeer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reindeer "Reindeer") herders, while the southern Yakuts raised [cattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakutian_cattle "Yakutian cattle") and [horses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakutian_horse "Yakutian horse").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTELevinPotapov1956-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAntipin1963-48)
## History
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakuts&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: History")]
### Imperial Russia
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakuts&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Imperial Russia")]
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/Yakutka_v_prazdnichnom_nariade.jpg/250px-Yakutka_v_prazdnichnom_nariade.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Yakutka_v_prazdnichnom_nariade.jpg)Yakut woman in the 1890s
In the 1620s, the [Tsardom of Muscovy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsardom_of_Russia "Tsardom of Russia") began to move into their territory and annexed or settled down on it, imposed a fur tax and [managed to suppress several Yakut rebellions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genocide_of_indigenous_peoples#Russian_tsarist_conquest_of_Siberia "Genocide of indigenous peoples") between 1634 and 1642. The tsarist brutality in collection of the pelt tax (_yasak_) sparked a rebellion and aggression among the Yakuts and also [Tungusic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tungusic_languages "Tungusic languages")-speaking tribes along the River [Lena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lena_River "Lena River") in 1642. The [voivode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voivode "Voivode") Peter Golovin, leader of the tsarist forces, responded with a reign of terror: native settlements were torched and hundreds of people were killed. The Yakut population alone is estimated to have fallen by 70 percent between 1642 and 1682, mainly because of [smallpox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smallpox "Smallpox") and other [infectious diseases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infectious_disease "Infectious disease").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTERichards2003238-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeveneRoberts1999155-50)
The discovery of [gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold "Gold") and, later, the building of the [Trans-Siberian Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans-Siberian_Railway "Trans-Siberian Railway"), brought ever-increasing numbers of Russians into the region. By the 1820s almost all the Yakuts claimed to have converted to the [Russian Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Orthodox "Russian Orthodox") church, but they retained (and still retain) a number of tengri practices. Yakut literature began to rise in the late 19th century, and a national revival occurred in the early 20th century.
### Russian Civil War
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakuts&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Russian Civil War")]
The last conflict of the [Russian Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Civil_War "Russian Civil War"), known as the [Yakut Revolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakut_Revolt "Yakut Revolt"), occurred here when [Cornet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornet_\(military_rank\) "Cornet \(military rank\)") [Mikhail Korobeinikov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikhail_Korobeinikov "Mikhail Korobeinikov"), a [White Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_movement "White movement") officer, led an uprising and a last stand against the [Red Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Army "Red Army").
### Soviet Union
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakuts&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Soviet Union")]
In 1922, the new Soviet government named the area the [Yakut Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakut_Autonomous_Soviet_Socialist_Republic "Yakut Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic"). In the late 1920s through the late 1930s, Yakut people were systematically persecuted, when [Joseph Stalin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Stalin "Joseph Stalin") launched his collectivization campaign.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDavisHarrisonHowell2007141-51) It is possible that hunger and malnutrition during this period resulted in a decline in the Yakut total population from 240,500 in 1926 to 236,700 in 1959. By 1972, the population began to recover.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTELewis2012-52)
### Russian Federation
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakuts&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Russian Federation")]
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e9/Yakuts_in_Yakutia_raions_percentage_2010.svg/250px-Yakuts_in_Yakutia_raions_percentage_2010.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Yakuts_in_Yakutia_raions_percentage_2010.svg)The percentage of Yakuts in the districts of [Yakutia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sakha_Republic "Sakha Republic"), in the 2010 census
Currently, Yakuts form a large plurality of the total population within the vast [Republic of Sakha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sakha_Republic "Sakha Republic"). According to the [2021 Russian census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Census_\(2021\) "Russian Census \(2021\)"), there were a total of 469,348 Yakuts residing in the Sakha Republic during that year, or 55.3% of the total population of the Republic.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-census2021-53)
## Culture
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakuts&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Culture")]
See also: [Yakutian knife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakutian_knife "Yakutian knife") and [Olonkho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olonkho "Olonkho")
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Sakha_woman.jpg/250px-Sakha_woman.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sakha_woman.jpg)A Yakut woman in traditional dress
The Yakuts engage in animal husbandry, traditionally having focused on rearing [horses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horse "Horse"), mainly the [Yakutian horse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakutian_horse "Yakutian horse"), [reindeer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reindeer_in_Russia "Reindeer in Russia") and the _Sakha Ynagha_ ('[Yakutian cow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakutian_cattle "Yakutian cattle")'), a hardy kind of [cattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cattle "Cattle") known as [Yakutian cattle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakutian_cattle "Yakutian cattle") which is well adapted to the harsh local weather.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKantanen2012-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMeerson-55) There is a widespread notion among other ethnic minorities in [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia") based on their experience (for example, among geographically close Mongolic [Buryats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buryats "Buryats")) that the Sakha (i.e. Yakuts) are the least [russified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russification "Russification") ethnic group in Russia and that the knowledge of the native language is widespread, particularly (as is often said) due to the cold and freezing nature of their geographical habitat, and [Russians'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russians "Russians") general avoidance of colonizing those lands.
Certain [rock formations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_formation "Rock formation") named [Kigilyakh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kigilyakh "Kigilyakh"), as well as places such as [Ynnakh Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ynnakh_Mountain "Ynnakh Mountain"), are held in high esteem by Yakuts.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAndreyevich2020-56)

According to the 2010 census, some 87% of the Yakuts in the Sakha Republic are fluent in the [Yakut (or Sakha) language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sakha_language "Sakha language"), while 90% are fluent in Russian.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTERussia2010b-57) The Sakha/Yakut language belongs to the Northern branch of the [Siberian Turkic languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siberian_Turkic_languages "Siberian Turkic languages"). ## DNA and genetics analysis
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yakuts&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: DNA and genetics analysis")]
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c0/Yakut_Sakha_hunter.jpg/250px-Yakut_Sakha_hunter.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Yakut_Sakha_hunter.jpg)A Yakut hunter, early 20th century
The primary [Y-chromosome DNA haplogroup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Y-chromosome_DNA_haplogroup "Human Y-chromosome DNA haplogroup") for the Yakut is [N-M231](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haplogroup_N-M231 "Haplogroup N-M231"). While found in around 89% of the general population,[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKhar'kovStepanovMedvedevSpiridonova2008-46) in northern Yakutia it is closer to 82%. N-M231 is shared with various other Eastern Siberian populations.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFedorovaReidlaMetspaluMetspalu2013-58) The remaining haplogroups are approximately: 4% [C-M217](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haplogroup_C-M217 "Haplogroup C-M217") (including subclades [C-M48](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haplogroup_C-M48 "Haplogroup C-M48") and C-M407), 3.5% [R1a-M17](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haplogroup_R1a "Haplogroup R1a") (including subclade R1a-M458), and 2.1% [N-P43](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haplogroup_N-M231#N1a2b_\(P43\) "Haplogroup N-M231"), with sporadic instances of [I-M253](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haplogroup_I-M253 "Haplogroup I-M253"), [R1b-M269](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haplogroup_R1b "Haplogroup R1b"), [J2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haplogroup_J-M172 "Haplogroup J-M172"), and [Q](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haplogroup_Q-M242 "Haplogroup Q-M242").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDugganWhittenWiebeCrawford2013-59)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFedorovaReidlaMetspaluMetspalu2013-58)
According to Adamov, [haplogroup N1c1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haplogroup_N_\(Y-DNA\)#Haplogroup_N1c1_\(N-M178\) "Haplogroup N \(Y-DNA\)") makes up 94% of the Sakha population. This genetic bottleneck has been dated approximately to AD 1300 ± 200 and it is proposed to have been caused by high mortality rates in warfare and later relocation to the Middle Lena River.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAdamov2008652-60)
The primary [mitochondrial DNA haplogroups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_mitochondrial_DNA_haplogroup "Human mitochondrial DNA haplogroup") are various East Asian lineages, making up 92% of the total: [haplogroup C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haplogroup_C_\(mtDNA\) "Haplogroup C \(mtDNA\)") at 36% to 45.7% and [haplogroup D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haplogroup_D_\(mtDNA\) "Haplogroup D \(mtDNA\)") at 25.7% to 32.9% of the Yakut.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFedorovaReidlaMetspaluMetspalu2013-58) Minor Eastern Eurasian mtDNA haplogroups include: 5.2% [G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haplogroup_G_\(mtDNA\) "Haplogroup G \(mtDNA\)"), 4.49% [F](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haplogroup_F_\(mtDNA\) "Haplogroup F \(mtDNA\)"), 3.55% [M13a1b](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haplogroup_M_\(mtDNA\) "Haplogroup M \(mtDNA\)"), 1.89% [A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haplogroup_A_\(mtDNA\) "Haplogroup A \(mtDNA\)"), 1.18% [Y1a](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haplogroup_Y_\(mtDNA\) "Haplogroup Y \(mtDNA\)"), 1.18% [B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haplogroup_B_\(mtDNA\) "Haplogroup B \(mtDNA\)"), 0.95% [Z3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haplogroup_Z_\(mtDNA\) "Haplogroup Z \(mtDNA\)"), and 0.71% [M7](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haplogroup_M_\(mtDNA\) "Haplogroup M \(mtDNA\)").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFedorovaReidlaMetspaluMetspalu2013-58) According to Fedorova, besides East Asian maternal lineages, "the mtDNA pool of the native populations of Sakha contains a small (8%), but diverse set of western Eurasian mtDNA haplogroups, mostly present among Yakuts and Evenks", the most common being H and J.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFedorovaReidlaMetspaluMetspalu2013-58)
According to a 2026 study, the genetic makeup of historical Yakuts from c. 1500 to 1922 was relatively homogenous and closely resembled that of modern Yakuts. Except for rare outliers, they can be modeled as a two-way admixture between populations that inhabited Iron Age Yakutia and the Baikal region from the thirteenth to fifteenth centuries. The Russian conquest of Yakutia also left minimal genetic impact on Yakuts. Overall, Yakuts cluster closer with Asian populations, especially Evenki, Ulchi and Buryats, than European or American populations.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-61)
Several genetic studies also state that Neolithic populations from Yakutia had [Ancient Paleo-Siberian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Paleo-Siberian "Ancient Paleo-Siberian") affinities and formed a genetic substratum for modern Siberian populations.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-62)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-64)

"_The Sakha people had made a temporary footprint in the U.S. in 1820 at Fort Ross[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-66) in Jenner, California. According to the 1820 census,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-67) five Sakha men lived in the fort with 260 people, working for the [Russian-American Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian-American_Company "Russian-American Company"), a fur-trading business. This fort became a melting pot of different cultures, including Russians, Native Alaskans and local Native American tribes, such as the Kashaya Pomo. The Sakha were part of the diverse workforce that supported the fort operations in areas, such as hunting, trapping, farming and construction. By 1860, there were at least 20 Sakhas living at Fort Ross before the Russian-American Company ended its North American operations in the early 1880s._" - Lynnwood Today [[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yakuts#cite_note-auto-65)
